Two phrases or sections overlap, so the last chord of one is also the first of the next and no gap separates them.
A chord that belongs to both the old key and the new one, used as a hinge to modulate smoothly.
Moving to a distant key by holding one note shared by both harmonies, which is heard afresh as a different member of the new chord.
Changing key without preparation: a phrase ends in one key and the next simply begins in another.
Respelling a note or chord — D♭ as C♯, say — so that it leads to a different key from the one its first spelling implied.
Moving a note or chord by a semitone to reach new harmonic ground, without a conventional modulation.
A short melodic or harmonic pattern repeated at a higher or lower pitch, usually several times in a row.
A held or repeated dominant note in the bass: the music waits for the tonic that it promises.
A held or repeated tonic note in the bass: the harmony moves above it, but the music stays at home.
The passage that prepares the return of the opening material, typically by lingering on the dominant of the home key.
Holding dominant harmony for a long stretch, so that a return or arrival is delayed and expected.
Stripping a theme down, motif by motif, until only a fragment or a single chord is left, often before a return.
A small motif carried across a join, so the new section feels derived from the old even when key, texture and tempo change.
A sign, an arc over a dot, that holds a note or rest beyond its written length; the performer decides how long.
Silence for the whole ensemble at once: a deliberate break that stops the music before it restarts.
The pause in a sonata exposition that separates the first group from the second theme, usually after a half cadence on the dominant.
